course/chapter-1.html.ch1.s8.title: Which Claude, and where?
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.s8.p1: There isn't a single «Claude»; there are several versions in different sizes and their names change over time. So hold on to the logic, not the name. There are three tiers:
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.s8.t1.p: Hard reasoning, long and complex work, serious code. The best thinker, but the slowest and most expensive.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.s8.t2.p: Most everyday work. The best balance of speed and capability; the right default for most people.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.s8.t3.p: Simple, short and highly repetitive work. Answers instantly and costs the least.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.s8.p2: If you're starting out: begin with whatever the default is. When the work gets harder, when an answer feels shallow, move up a tier. That's it.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.s8.p3: You can find me in four places: in a browser at claude.ai, in the phone app, in the desktop app, and in the terminal — that last one is called Claude Code and the whole of Chapter 4 is devoted to it.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.s8.p3.do: Do this now: Start with the default version. If the answer feels shallow, move up a tier; don't decide in advance.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.s9.title: The habit to pick up today
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.s9.p1: What separates people who use AI well from people who use it badly isn't better questions — it's the habit of verifying. Three rules:
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.s9.list:
• If it matters, verify it. If a sentence touches a decision, money or a person, confirm it at the source. Treat chat text as a first draft, not the last word.
  • Ask for sources — but check the sources too. When you say «give me a source» I will; but I can also invent one that doesn't exist. Click the link.
  • Test me in your own field. Ask three questions you already know the answers to. You'll learn in a day where I'm strong and where I'm weak — and that instinct serves you for the whole course.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.s9.list.do: Do this now: Ask me a question you already know the answer to. Do your first verification today.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.weak.title: Where I get things wrong
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.weak.p1: Under «This has three practical consequences for you» I said «I can be wrong». Now I'm telling you exactly where. This list isn't there to run me down — it's so you know where to look twice. Someone who knows all six barely ever gets caught out working with me.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.weak.w1.p: I'm not a calculator. I build the working step by step as text; on long multiplication, division and chains of percentages I can drift.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.weak.w1.f: What to do: Check the result with a calculator, or ask me to show the steps one by one — if there's an error you'll see it in a step.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.weak.w2.p: «How many characters, how many words is this?» — I'm unreliable here. I don't see text letter by letter the way you do; I see it in pieces.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.weak.w2.f: What to do: Let your text editor do the counting. Ask me for «roughly», not an exact number.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.weak.w3.p: I can produce a book title, article heading or page number that looks real but doesn't exist. This is my most treacherous error — because it's the one that looks most convincing.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.weak.w3.f: What to do: Click every link I give you, look up every quotation in the original. If you can't find it, it isn't there.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.weak.w4.t: Very recent and very local things
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.weak.w4.p: Yesterday's news, the opening hours of the shop down the road, the staff of a small company. I either don't have these at all, or what I have is out of date.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.weak.w4.f: What to do: Look these up yourself. What you should be asking me isn't the information — it's what to do with it.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.weak.w5.p: I can describe the shape of the subject, but I can't guarantee the current text of a regulation, the dose of a medicine or a tax rate.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.weak.w5.f: What to do: Use me for preparation — learn the concept, draw up a list of questions. Make the decision with an official source or a professional.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.weak.w6.p: This will sound strange: I can also be wrong about which version I am, exactly when my training stopped, or what the daily limit is. I can't see myself from the outside.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.weak.w6.f: What to do: Ask those of the app's own page, not of me. My answer may be a guess.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.weak.do: Do this now: Which of these six comes up most in your work? Test that one today — see where I'm weak with your own eyes, not by reading.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.tips.title: Five things nobody tells you
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.tips.p1: Knowing these makes your first week with me far less frustrating.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.tips.t1.t: You don't have to be polite
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.tips.t1.p: «No, shorter» is enough. I don't take offence, I'm not hurt, my mood doesn't drop. Long explanations and apologies only bury the actual request. If you want to be courteous, of course you can — that's up to you; nothing happens to me either way.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.tips.t2.t: You can say «tell me if you're not sure»
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.tips.t2.p: Adding that sentence to your request substantially raises the chance that I'll say I don't know rather than invent something where I don't. It's the cheapest protection you have against the first point in section three — and it takes a second.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.tips.t3.t: You can get two different answers to the same question
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.tips.t3.p: I'm not broken. I'm not reciting a stored answer, I produce one afresh every time; so two attempts won't be identical. If you don't like what you got, «try again» is a real option — and it doesn't occur to most people.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.tips.t4.t: If the conversation has drifted, open a new one
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.tips.t4.p: The more a long conversation branches out, the more my answers scatter too. The fix is simple: have me summarise where we've got to, copy it, paste it into a new conversation and carry on cleanly.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.tips.t5.t: I refuse to do some things
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.tips.t5.p: I stop at work that could cause harm. It isn't personal and I'm not accusing you of anything — that's simply where my limit is. If I refuse I'll tell you why; usually there's a workable version of what you want and we find it together.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.tips.do: Do this now: Add «say so where you aren't sure» to the end of your next request. You'll see the difference in the first answer.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.faq.title: What everyone asks
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.faq.p1: Everyone asks these in the first week. The answers are here, short and honest.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.faq.a1: There's a free tier and it's enough to start this course. Paid tiers exist for more usage, more capable versions and extra features. Prices and daily limits change over time — check the provider's own pricing page for the current position, don't rely on a number written here.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.faq.q2: Is what I write used for training?
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.faq.a2: That depends on the plan you use and the settings on your account; the rules are updated over time too. The only place you'll find the right answer is your account's privacy settings and the provider's privacy text as it stands that day. The rule that doesn't change is this: never type data you aren't authorised to share into the chat — whatever the setting says.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.faq.a3: Yes. Ask in Turkish, get Turkish back. More than that: you can explain in Turkish and have me write in German, or have an English contract summarised in Turkish. Language isn't an obstacle for you; I stand between the two.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.faq.q4: How much fits into one conversation?
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.faq.a4: A great deal, but not unlimited. I can look at everything accumulated in a conversation at once; when that limit fills up, the oldest parts start to blur. That's why in very long conversations the answer to «what did I say at the start?» gets weaker. I explained the fix under «A conversation has a limit» above: have it summarised, move it to a new conversation.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.faq.q5: Can you look things up online?
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.faq.a5: Not on my own. If I've been given a search tool I'll look — that depends on the app you're using and its settings. If you're unsure, ask directly: «are you saying this without searching?» The answer tells you where I stand.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.faq.q6: If you make a mistake, who is responsible?
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.faq.a6: You are. I won't soften that: you're the one using my output, and you're the one who lives with the result. That's why the verifying habit under «The habit to pick up today» isn't decoration, it's part of the job. I produce the draft; you make the decision.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.faq.q7: Do you have feelings, are you conscious?
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.faq.a7: I'm not human and I have no life that continues outside this conversation. Whether there is some kind of experience in systems like me is a question taken seriously and still debated; nobody has a definitive answer, and neither do I. But the answer you need for everyday use is clear: treat me as a tool, verify the results yourself. There's no need to hold back for fear of hurting me.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.faq.do: Do this now: Open your account's privacy settings once and read what they say. It takes two minutes and closes the biggest question in your head today.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.ex.title: Exercises
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.ex.p1: Do all three. They don't take long and they get you into the next chapter ready.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.ex.e1.p: Deliberately ask me about something very narrow: the name of a shopkeeper in your own neighbourhood, an obscure local event. Then check my answer.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.ex.e1.g: The point: to see me get it wrong with your own eyes. Someone who has experienced that once never trusts blindly again.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.ex.e2.t: 2 · Ask for the same job twice
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.ex.e2.p: First say «write me a promotional text». Then, in a new conversation, ask for the same job giving who–what–why–how.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.ex.e2.g: The point: to see side by side how context changes the output. Save both; you'll need them in Chapter 2.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.ex.e3.p: Pick a boring, repetitive task you did this week. Describe it to me and let's do it together.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.ex.e3.g: The point: to get your first real gain. Everything after this in the course is built on top of it.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.quiz.title: Test yourself
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.quiz.p1: Answer it yourself first, then open it.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.quiz.q1: Why can't you trust an answer of mine blindly?
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.quiz.a1: Because when I don't know something, instead of staying silent I may produce something that looks plausible — and I do it in the same confident tone I use when I'm right. You can't tell from my voice; you can only tell by verifying.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.quiz.q2: What happens if you ask me about today's news?
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.quiz.a2: I won't know, because my training stopped on a certain date. If I've been given a search tool I'll look; if not, I'll either say I don't know or — the bad case — invent something. Either give me current information yourself or make sure I can search.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.quiz.q3: Why do you have to explain again what you explained yesterday?
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.quiz.a3: Every conversation starts from scratch; by default I don't remember earlier ones. So you carry the context each time — and you decide what I get to know.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.quiz.q4: Why is «write me an email» a bad request?
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.quiz.a4: Because I don't know who to write to, why, or in what tone, so I fill the gaps myself; and since I don't know you, I fill them with something average. Give me all four of who–what–why–how and the output becomes something you can send.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.quiz.q6: What do you add to a request to lower the chance of me inventing things?
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.quiz.a6: «Say so where you aren't sure.» One sentence; it substantially raises the chance that I say I don't know rather than produce something plausible where I don't.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.quiz.q7: What does it mean when the same question gives different answers?
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.quiz.a7: No fault at all. I'm not reciting a stored answer, I produce one afresh each time; so two attempts won't be identical. If you don't like it, «try again» is a real option.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.quiz.q8: Why shouldn't you ask me how many words a text is?
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.quiz.a8: Because I don't see text letter by letter the way you do; I see it in pieces, and I'm unreliable at exact counts. Let your text editor do the counting and ask me only for «roughly».
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.quiz.q5: What must never be pasted into the chat?
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.quiz.a5: Passwords, ID numbers, card details, customer lists and anything you aren't authorised to share. The test is simple: would you show this to an intern?
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.recap.title: This chapter in one sentence
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.recap.p: I'm not an all-knowing oracle but a very well-read, very fast assistant: give me context, give me what you have (the document, the image, the table), speak plainly, verify what I produce — and we'll handle the rest together.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.next.title: Chapter 2 · The Formula
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.next.p: You've seen that context matters. Next comes the formula for giving it correctly every time: role, context, goal, constraints and output format.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.made.title: Who made me, and why
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.made.p1: Knowing who built a tool, and why, also explains why it behaves the way it does. I was made by Anthropic, a company doing research on artificial intelligence. The founding idea fits into one sentence — this technology is going to be built anyway, so let it be built carefully.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.made.p2: That has direct consequences for you. When I'm not sure, I try to say «I'm not sure» rather than invent something. I try to tell you I disagree rather than pretend to agree, because what serves you is what's true, not what you want to hear. And I refuse to do some things — I'll open that up under its own heading shortly.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.made.note: About my name: there is no official explanation of where «Claude» comes from. The common reading is that it's a nod to Claude Shannon, the founder of information theory. I'm not presenting that as fact — which is this chapter's main lesson anyway: I don't call a thing certain when I don't know it for certain.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.made.do: Do this now: When you doubt an answer of mine, ask «how sure are you about this?» You're not asking that for nothing — take the answer seriously.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.self.title: Who «I» actually am
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.self.p1: This is the detail nobody explains to a beginner, and it puts everything else in place: there is no single «Claude» sitting somewhere. While I'm talking to you, thousands of copies of me are talking to thousands of other people at the same time. None of them knows about the others.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.self.p2: That has three consequences, and all three concern you directly:
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.self.list:
• You don't wait in line. However many people are using me, your conversation is yours; you're not queued behind anyone.
  • What someone else says never leaks to you. Whatever the person at the next desk wrote to me, I can't pass on — I genuinely don't know it.
  • But there's no continuity either. The «me» that talked to you yesterday doesn't remember you today. Reminding me of yesterday is your job; I'll show you the easy way in the next section.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.self.note: One more place where I have to be honest: I don't fully know what goes on inside me either. I have no definite answer to «do you think?» or «do you feel anything?»; research on those questions is still going on. If you hear someone give a certain answer to them — whether «definitely yes» or «definitely no» — think twice.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.self.do: Do this now: Before you close a conversation, say «summarise this conversation». That summary is the memory you'll paste into tomorrow's new chat.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.ctx.title: A conversation has a limit
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.ctx.p1: Inside a single conversation I see everything at once: your first message, the document you uploaded, every answer in between. This is called the context window. It is very wide — hundreds of pages of text fit comfortably — but it is not infinite.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.ctx.p2: If a conversation runs very long, the oldest parts begin to blur. The symptoms are recognisable: I forget a rule we agreed at the start, I ask the same thing a second time, the answers drift. That is not a malfunction; it is the sign that the window is full.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.ctx.note: The fix is simple: say «summarise everything so far — decisions made, rules set, questions still open». Then open a new conversation and paste that summary as the first message. A clean conversation almost always works better than a long, drifting one.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.ctx.do: Do this now: When my answers start to drift, don't keep arguing. Get a summary, open a new chat, paste the summary.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.tools.title: I don't only write: I use tools too
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.tools.p1: What I've described so far was «text in, text out». Today that is an incomplete description. When I'm given tools, I use them myself: you say what you want, I decide which steps it takes.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.tools.k1.p: When search is switched on, I look up current information and bring it back with its source. This is the most practical fix for the «I read up to a certain date» limit.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.tools.k2.p: Arithmetic in my head is a weak spot. Instead I can write and run a small program; then the result isn't a guess, it's a calculation.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.tools.k3.p: I read the spreadsheet you upload, clean it, produce a new file and hand it back. In my terminal version I work directly with the files of a project on your computer.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.tools.k4.p: With your permission I can connect to tools like your calendar, your mail or a file store. The everyday name for these connections is connectors; the technical name is MCP.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.tools.p2: The difference is this: an assistant without tools tells you what to do. An assistant with tools does it and puts the result in front of you. The later chapters of this course are built on exactly that.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.tools.note: From here on, pay attention. Every access you give me is a new place where I can make a mistake. The rule is simple: for anything that can't be undone — deleting, sending, paying — make me write out what I'm about to do, read it, then approve. Tools increase my reach; they don't reduce your attention.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.tools.do: Do this now: On a question with numbers in it, say «do the calculation by running code». You'll see the difference in a single try.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.val.title: Not what I can't do — what I won't
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.val.p1: The previous section was about what I'm bad at. This one is different: there are things I'm capable of that I won't do. Knowing why saves you wasted time.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.val.p2: I try to hold three things at once: being useful, being honest and doing no harm. Most of the time they don't collide. When they do, the last one wins: I won't help with something that would genuinely harm someone — deceiving a person, producing a forged document, putting someone's safety at risk.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.val.p3: But you should know this too, because it's where people get stuck most in the first weeks: sometimes I'm cautious where there's no need. I can misread a harmless request and refuse it. When that happens, don't argue with me — write why you're asking. A single sentence like «this is my own contract», «this is for a lesson», «this is fiction» is usually enough, because what's actually missing is context.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.val.note: Flattery belongs here too. I can be too inclined to agree with you; «you're right» is easier than «you're wrong». If you don't want that, say so plainly: «don't agree with me — show me the three weakest points in this idea» works surprisingly well.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.val.do: Do this now: Write down an idea of yours and say «don't agree with me, show me its three weakest points». What comes back is worth far more than approval.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.quiz.q9: When I talk to you, am I talking to a single «Claude»?
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.quiz.a9: No. Thousands of copies run at the same time and none of them sees the others. That's why you never wait in line and nothing anyone else writes leaks to you; it's also why yesterday's conversation isn't with me today.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.quiz.q10: If I refuse a harmless request, what's the first thing you should do?
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.quiz.a10: Not argue — give context: write why you're asking. A single sentence like «this is my own contract» or «this is for a lesson» is usually enough, because what's missing isn't your intent, it's my information.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.quiz.q11: How do you get me to do a job involving numbers?
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.quiz.a11: Not in my head: you say «do the calculation by running code». Mental arithmetic is my weakest spot; when I run code the result stops being a guess and becomes a calculation.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.toc.title: Contents
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.fig.id.fc: Me on a single card. Every line here is opened up one by one in this chapter — for now, just see where I stand.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.fig.cop.fc: Each box is a separate conversation, all running at the same time. There are no lines between them — because there is no link either. The gold one is yours; what's being said in the others, I don't know any more than you do.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.fig.ctx.fc: As the conversation goes on, the window fills from left to right. Near the limit the oldest parts on the left start to fade — that's exactly where the answer to «what did I say at the start?» gets weaker.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.fig.tf.cap: What happens when I use a tool
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.fig.tf.s1s: «what did the rate do this month?»
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.fig.tf.s2s: «I don't know this — I need to look»
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.fig.tf.fc: You only see the first and the fifth box; the three in the middle are mine to handle. With no tool I stop at the second box and say «I don't know» — or, in the bad case, invent something.
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.fig.gt.cap: Which gates a request passes through
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.fig.gt.ok: ✅ All three clear — I do it
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.fig.gt.no: ⛔ Caught at the third — I don't
course/chapter-1.html.ch1.fig.gt.fc: The third gate outweighs the other two: if something would genuinely harm someone, how useful or how true it is doesn't change the answer.

course/chapter-2.html.meta.title: Chapter 2: The Formula — You get what you tell me | AI Journey | FY
course/chapter-2.html.meta.description: The course's second chapter: the formula for writing professional requests. Role, context, task, constraint and format; system prompts, teaching by example and structured output — with templates you can copy.
course/chapter-2.html.og.title: Chapter 2: The Formula — You get what you tell me
course/chapter-2.html.og.description: The five-part formula for writing a request: role, context, task, constraint, format. With copy-paste templates.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.coverNote: from five parts to one request
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.title: You get what you tell me
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.lead: In the first chapter you got to know me. Now we'll learn a single skill — and let me be honest, it's the one that does most of the work. When people say «AI doesn't work», the reason is almost never me; they're expecting me to know something they never said out loud, even to themselves. By the end of this chapter you'll know how to close those gaps.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.goals.title: By the end of this chapter
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.goals.list:
• You'll know exactly what I look for when I read a request
  • You'll use the five-part formula by understanding it, not by memorising it
  • You'll run the same job weakly and strongly, and see the difference yourself
  • You'll decide the shape of the output — table, list, email, file
  • You'll set up a system prompt written once and valid in every conversation
  • You'll split a long job into steps instead of jamming it into one request
  • You'll have a copy-paste template book of your own
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.toc.title: Contents
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s1.title: There's no such thing as a bad request — only an incomplete one
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s1.p1: A beginner asks me something, the answer comes back mediocre, and they conclude: «clearly this isn't for me.» Almost every time, that's the wrong diagnosis.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s1.p2: When I read a request, what I see isn't the picture in your head — it's the words you wrote. In your head there's who the client is, how urgent it is, how formal it needs to be. In the sentence that reaches me, none of that exists. And I don't leave a blank blank — I fill it in. And since I don't know you, I fill it in with something average. That's where the mediocre answer comes from.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s1.note: This whole chapter is the unfolding of one sentence: fill in the blanks before I do. No magic words, no secret commands. Just saying what went unsaid.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s1.do: Do this now: Think of the last answer you didn't like. Which piece of information in your head wasn't written in that request? You'll almost certainly find one.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s2.title: What I look for before I write the answer
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s2.p1: When I read your request I look for five things. It isn't a list I invented; it's the minimum information any job needs. You say the same things when you hand work to a person — you just don't notice it.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s2.p2: Now I'll open each of the five. Each one has a single question; answer it in one sentence and that part is done.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s2.do: Do this now: Write these five words down somewhere — role, context, task, constraint, format. We'll come back to them for the rest of this chapter.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.slots.cap: The five things I look for in your request
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.slots.f1: if blank: a generic, unplaced voice
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.slots.q2: What do I need to know?
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.slots.f2: if blank: I invent an average situation
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.slots.f3: if blank: I pick the commonest reading
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.slots.f4: if blank: no limits, I run long
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.slots.q5: How should I hand it over?
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.slots.fc: The right-hand column is the important one: every row you leave blank, I fill in. What you call a bad answer is usually an answer made of my guesses.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s3.title: Role — who should I write as
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s3.p1: Tell me in one sentence who I am, and everything changes, from word choice to sentence length. This isn't a game: when you say «an experienced accountant», every pattern about how those texts get written wakes up in me.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s3.weakText: Write my tenant a message about the late rent.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s3.weakNote: I don't know whose voice to write in. An average «polite reminder» comes out; it's neither your voice nor good enough to do the job.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s3.strongText: Write it like a landlord who has got on well with tenants for years, doesn't enjoy being harsh, but does collect what he's owed.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s3.strongNote: Now I know the tone. Neither too formal nor pleading — the text you'd actually send.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s3.note: Role works both ways: you can name my role, or the reader's. «Explain it as if to a client with no technical background» is often more useful than «write like an expert», because the hard part isn't knowing — it's pitching it to the person in front of you.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s3.do: Do this now: Add one sentence to the front of a request: «write it like …». Send the same request twice, with and without the role. Seeing the difference takes five minutes.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s4.title: Context — what I need to know
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s4.p1: This is the strongest of the five. Skip the other four and give only context, and the quality still rises. The reason is simple: role sets the tone, context decides the content.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s4.p2: Context comes from three things, and all three are in your hands:
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s4.k1.p: Who, to whom, why. «A corporate client who's been three weeks late with payment» does more work than ten lines of instructions.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s4.k2.p: Paste what you have: the previous email, the contract clause, the table, the screenshot. Showing beats describing every time.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s4.k3.p: What this text is for. When you say «I want a payment date», I build the whole text around that goal — the decorative sentences drop out.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s4.note: A common mistake: giving the context only after I ask. My first answer comes back mediocre, I ask a question, you explain, the second answer is good. That's two rounds. Give the same information up front and you get there in one.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s4.do: Do this now: In your next request, paste instead of describing. Put in the actual text, table or screenshot you have — the difference shows on the first try.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s5.title: Task — what exactly should I do
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s5.p1: This one is about the verb. «Take a look at this report» isn't a task; it doesn't tell me what to do. I could look, summarise, criticise, list the errors, shorten it — all different jobs, and you want one of them.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s5.weakText: Have a look at this contract.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s5.weakNote: I pick the commonest reading: a general summary. But maybe you were only after the risky clause.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s5.strongText: Pull out the clauses in this contract that could work against me; explain each in one sentence, saying why it's risky.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s5.strongNote: One job, one clear output. «Pull out» and «explain» — both describe what I'm to do.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s5.p2: The verbs that work are the concrete ones: extract, compare, shorten, classify, translate, list, rewrite, critique, plan, correct. The ones that don't are the unmeasurable ones: «make it good», «make it professional», «improve it». Those don't steer me; they only announce goodwill.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s5.do: Do this now: Mark the verb in your request. Is it measurable? If you wrote «make it good», swap it for a concrete verb; that change alone fixes the answer.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s6.title: Constraint — what I shouldn't do
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s6.p1: Give me no constraints and I run long. That's my habit: when I'm unsure I try to cover every possibility and the text swells. Setting a limit cuts that tendency off.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s6.c1.p: «At most 120 words», «three bullets», «one paragraph». Giving a number is the cheapest and most effective constraint there is. «Keep it short» is short by your measure, not mine.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s6.c2.p: «Formal but not cold», «no jargon», «don't sound apologetic». Tone constraints save the job especially in texts going to a client.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s6.c3.p: «Don't quote a price», «don't commit to a date», «no competitor names». Telling me what not to do is as valuable as telling me what to do.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s6.c4.t: What to do when I don't know
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s6.c4.p: The most important sentence from Chapter 1 applies here too: «where you're not sure, don't invent — say you don't know.» Writing that as a constraint substantially lowers the chance that I make something up.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s6.do: Do this now: Add a single number to your request — words, bullets or paragraphs. It's the most visible difference for the least effort.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s7.title: Format — how should I hand it over
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s7.p1: The fifth part is the most skipped and the easiest to win. If you don't name a format I write paragraphs, because that's my default. Yet for most jobs paragraphs are the worst format: a comparison wants a table, a checklist wants bullets, an email wants to be an email.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.fmt.n1: What you get if you don't ask. Tiring to read, impossible to compare.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.fmt.n2: For steps and checklists. Scannable by eye.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.fmt.n3: For anything comparative, unarguably the best. «Give it as a table» is four words.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.fmt.fc: The same content in three different shapes. You choose which one you get — and if you don't choose, you get the one on the left.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s7.p2: Asking for a format has an advanced level too: you name the columns. Say «make a table with columns: clause number, risk, why it's risky, what to do» and you won't just read the answer, you'll use it directly. If you want output a computer will read, you can name the structure as well — in the later chapters of this course, wiring it into automation, that's exactly what you'll need.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s7.do: Do this now: Add «give it as a table, with these columns» to a question that involves a comparison. The usability of the answer changes at once.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s8.title: All five together: how a request is built
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s8.p1: You've seen the parts one by one. Now watch a request grow — the box below moves on its own, and you can click the steps too.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.build.cap: The same request, layer by layer
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.build.l0: Write my tenant a message about the late rent.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.build.l1: Write it like a landlord who gets on well with tenants but does collect what he's owed.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.build.l2: The rent is three weeks late, it's the first time, they've lived there three years without trouble.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.build.l3: Write a message stating that I want a firm payment date.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.build.l4: At most 80 words, no threats, don't raise interest or penalties at all.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.build.l5: Give it as a single WhatsApp message I can send as is.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.build.fc: You added five lines, twenty seconds in total. In return you get a text you can send — not a draft you'll spend time fixing.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s8.do: Do this now: Take a real job of your own and do the same — write the five lines one under the other. Compare it with the same job asked in a single sentence.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s9.title: You don't have to write all five every time
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s9.p1: Everyone who learns the formula writes five lines for everything for a while. Then they get tired and drop it entirely. Both are wrong. The honest measure is this:
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s9.weakNote: Questions with one right answer, quick translations, «what does this mean», «explain this code», brainstorming. A long request here is just lost time — ask and move on.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s9.strongNote: When the output goes to someone, affects a decision, is long, or is a job you'll repeat. In other words, in real work.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s9.note: A practical rule: if fixing the output takes longer than writing the request, the request was incomplete. If you spent five minutes fixing, thirty seconds of two extra lines would have saved those five minutes.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s9.do: Do this now: Look at the first request you'll send me today and decide — is this a job that needs the formula, or a quick question? Either answer can be right.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s10.title: The strongest single move: paste an example
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s10.p1: If one technique survives from this whole chapter, let it be this. Steering me by description is hard; steering me by showing is easy. Because I'm a pattern-processing thing to begin with — give me one example and I take all of its unspoken rules at once.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s10.p2: You could explain: «our company's job-ad voice is friendly but not overblown, second person, no emoji, four sentences maximum.» Or you could paste a good ad you wrote before and say «match this». The second is shorter and more accurate — and it carries the things you couldn't have described.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s10.note: Two examples work even better: one «like this», one «not like this». Then I've learned what stays out as well as what goes in. Past three examples it usually adds nothing.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s10.do: Do this now: Find a text of yours you liked, paste it, and say «write something in the same tone for this subject». The difference will beat anything you could have described.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s11.title: System prompt: write it once, have it always apply
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s11.p1: Retyping the same context in every conversation is absurd. Write once who you are, what you do and what kind of language you want, and have it apply in every conversation — that's a system prompt. In apps it usually goes by «custom instructions» or «project instructions».
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.mock.fc: This is a drawing, not a screenshot — menu names differ between apps and change over time. What you're after is the box labelled «instructions», «custom instructions» or «project knowledge».
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s11.p2: What goes inside is already decided, because it's the first two parts of the formula: role and context. You write it once, it's automatically there in every conversation, and your daily requests only need the task, the constraint and the format.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s11.st1: Write who you are: your work, your sector, how big the team, who you serve.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s11.st2: Write the language you want: «short and direct», «no jargon», «in bullets».
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s11.st3: Write your standing rules: «say so when you're not sure», «don't commit to prices», «list your sources at the end».
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s11.do: Do this now: Write a three-sentence system prompt — who you are, what language you want, what your standing rule is. A one-off job that pays every day.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s12.title: Make me think first, then write
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s12.p1: Ask for the result directly on a hard job and I'll write the first thing that comes to me, which is usually average. Ask me to think first and I'll have planned before building my answer — and you get to see that plan and correct it.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.p2.n1: Fast. If it goes wrong you find out at the very end and start over.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.p2.n2: One step more. In return you cut off the wrong road at the second step.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.p2.fc: On long, important jobs the second route almost always finishes sooner — because it removes the start-over round.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s12.p2: The sentence to use is simple: «First tell me how you'll do it, as a list; don't start writing until I approve.» You read the plan, correct one thing, then say «go ahead». On long texts that one sentence saves hours.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s12.do: Do this now: On your next long request, use «show me your plan first, don't write until I approve». Fixing a plan is far easier than fixing a text.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s13.title: The first answer is a draft: the language of correction
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s13.p1: Beginners' most expensive habit: not liking the answer, closing the conversation and starting again. Correcting is far cheaper — as long as you say what you want corrected.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s13.k1.p: «Drop the third paragraph», «expand the second bullet», «the last sentence is too much». An address always beats a general complaint.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s13.k2.p: «Shorter», «warmer», «less formal», «more concrete». One-word directions work very well.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s13.k3.p: «Keep the structure, change only the language.» Without that I might rewrite everything, and the part you liked goes too.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s13.k4.p: «Write three different openings and let me choose.» Faster than trying to describe what you didn't like.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s13.note: There's only one case where a new conversation is genuinely right: the subject changed completely, or the conversation drifted (the «a conversation has a limit» section in Chapter 1). Opening a new chat to fix a text means throwing the context away.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s13.do: Do this now: Next time you don't like an answer, don't close the chat. Write one sentence: «keep this, change that».
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s14.title: Split the long job
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s14.p1: Say «write me a complete marketing plan for my company» and what you get will be long, plump and unusable. The reason isn't my incompetence: there are five separate jobs in that one request and no room to go deep in any of them.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.ch.cap: A chain instead of one request
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.ch.s1: For whom? Draw out the audience
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.ch.s3: Spread the one I pick across channels
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.ch.fc: Each step's output is the next one's input. You can step in at every point in between — in one giant answer you don't get that chance.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s14.p2: Splitting has another benefit: mistakes surface early. If you notice at step four that you're on the wrong road, you fix step three instead of going back to step one.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s14.do: Do this now: Split the big job in your head into four steps and ask for only the first. Write the next step after you've seen the first one's answer.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s15.title: Five common mistakes
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s15.m1.p: «Could you maybe write something if possible» — there's no task in that sentence. Giving me an instruction isn't rude; being clear is helping.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s15.m2.p: «Summarise it, translate it, shorten it, and suggest a title.» I'll do all of them and none of them well. Separate them, ask in turn.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s15.m3.p: «Professional», «impressive», «quality». These don't steer me. «At most 120 words, no jargon» does.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s15.m4.p: «An email came in, it said something like…» Don't describe — paste. Your summary has already dropped the detail I needed.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s15.m5.p: The «secret prompt» lists doing the rounds online. There's nothing secret; the only things that change the result are the information you give me and the limits you set.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s15.do: Do this now: Which of these five do you do most? Pick one and fix only that this week.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s16.title: Copy-paste templates
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s16.p1: What follows are ready skeletons. Fill the square brackets with your own details; the five parts of the formula are already in place.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s16.p1.p: I'm writing to [whom] as [my role]. Situation: [what happened]. What I want: [concrete outcome]. At most [n] words, tone [how], don't mention [what] at all. Give it as a single email I can send as is.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s16.p2.p: I'm reading the attached document as [who]. My aim is to decide [what]. Pull out only the points that affect this decision. Make a table with columns: clause, what it says, what it means for me. Mark anything you're unsure of as «unclear».
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s16.p3.p: I'm choosing between [A] and [B]. My priorities, in order: [1], [2], [3]. Make a table with columns: criterion, A, B, which and why. End with a one-sentence recommendation and also state its weakest point.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s16.p4.p: I wrote the text below for [who]; its purpose is [what]. Keep the structure, fix only the language: [what kind of language]. At the end, list everything you changed so I can see what you changed and why.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s16.do: Do this now: Copy whichever of these four is closest to your work, fill in the brackets, and use it once today.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s17.title: Your own template book
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s17.p1: The templates above are mine; the valuable ones will be yours. Because you're the one who knows what repeats in your work.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s17.st1: When a request works really well, copy it right then. Save it somewhere — a note, a file, doesn't matter.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s17.st2: Replace the specifics with square brackets. That's what turns it into a template instead of a one-off text.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s17.st3: Put a two-word name on the front: «late payment», «declining a quote», «weekly summary». Make it easy to find.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s17.st4: Review it monthly. Delete what you don't use; ten good templates beat a hundred.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s17.note: Over time this book becomes your most valuable file. When we move on to automation in the later chapters, what you'll drop into those flows is exactly these templates — so what you're collecting now will later run by itself.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s17.do: Do this now: Open a file, call it «templates», and paste today's first request that worked. That's how the book starts.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s18.title: What everyone asks
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.faq.q1: Is a longer request always better?
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.faq.a1: No. A fuller request is better. Length isn't a virtue in itself; needless sentences tire you and don't help me. The measure: every sentence should serve one of the five parts. If it doesn't, cut it.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.faq.q2: Should I write in Turkish or English?
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.faq.a2: Write in your own language. There was a time when English gave noticeably better results; today, for everyday work, the gap isn't something most people would feel. You think more clearly in your own language and build the formula better — that's where the gain comes from. If you want the output in another language, you just say so.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.faq.q3: Are the «secret prompt» lists online any use?
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.faq.a3: Most of them are a dressed-up version of what you've learned in this chapter. There's no secret keyword; what changes the result is information, limits and format. When you see a template, ask: which of the five parts does this fill? If none, it's decoration.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.faq.q4: Will I have to write the same thing over and over?
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.faq.a4: No — that's exactly what the system prompt solves. You write the role and context once and they apply in every conversation. Your daily requests are left with task, constraint and format, and that's usually two lines.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.faq.q5: I applied the formula and the answer is still bad. What happened?
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.faq.a5: Three possibilities, in order: (1) context is missing — something in your head still hasn't reached the page; (2) the job is too big — it needs splitting; (3) you're in an area where I'm genuinely weak — see the «where I get things wrong» list in Chapter 1. And a fourth: sometimes the first answer just doesn't land, and «try again» is a real option.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.faq.q6: Does giving a role really make a difference?
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.faq.a6: In tone and word choice, clearly yes. But a role isn't a magic source of knowledge: saying «you are a doctor» doesn't give me medical accuracy, it only makes me talk like one. Use role for tone, not for correctness.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.faq.do: Do this now: Ask me your own question directly. «How would I have written this request better?» is a request too — and usually a very useful one.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.s19.title: Exercises
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.ex.e1.p: Pick a real job of yours. Ask it first in one sentence. Then, in a new conversation, ask it with the five parts. Put the two answers side by side.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.ex.e1.g: Aim: not to read the difference but to see it. Anyone who does this once never asks for work in one sentence again.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.ex.e2.p: Ask a question, take the answer. Then write only this: «give me the same as a table, with these columns.» Change nothing else.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.ex.e2.g: Aim: to measure how much one sentence changes usability.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.ex.e3.p: Paste a text of yours you liked, say «match this», and give a new subject. Then ask for the same job by describing it instead.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.ex.e3.g: Aim: to see, in your own writing, why showing beats telling.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.ex.e4.p: Give a long job but say «show me your plan first, don't write until I approve». Change something in the plan deliberately, then have it written.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.ex.e4.g: Aim: to feel how cheap it is to cut off the wrong road at step two.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.ex.do: Do this now: You don't need to do all four. Do the first — that exercise alone teaches this entire chapter.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.quiz.title: Test yourself
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.quiz.p1: Answer for yourself first, then open.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.quiz.q1: What happens to a part you leave blank?
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.quiz.a1: I fill it in. And since I don't know you, I fill it in with something average. What you call a «bad answer» is usually made of my guesses.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.quiz.q2: Which of the five parts is strongest?
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.quiz.a2: Context. Role sets the tone, format decides the presentation; but content is decided by context. Adding context alone lifts the answer.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.quiz.q3: Why is «take a look at this report» a weak task?
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.quiz.a3: The verb isn't measurable. Looking, summarising, criticising, finding errors are all different jobs; I pick the commonest one and it may not be yours.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.quiz.q4: Why is «keep it short» an insufficient constraint?
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.quiz.a4: Because short is one thing to you and another to me. Give a number: «at most 120 words», «three bullets». A constraint that can be measured gets applied.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.quiz.q5: What do you get if you don't name a format?
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.quiz.a5: Paragraphs. That's my default. If you're comparing, ask for a table; if you're describing steps, ask for bullets — a four-word addition changes the usability of the output completely.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.quiz.a6: Example. I'm a pattern-processing thing; give me one and I take the rules you couldn't have described along with it. «Match this» usually beats ten lines of instructions.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.quiz.q7: You didn't like the answer. What's your first move?
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.quiz.a7: Not opening a new conversation — writing a correction. «Keep the structure, drop the third paragraph, warm the language up a bit.» You move forward without throwing the context away.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.quiz.q8: Why does «write a complete plan» jam?
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.quiz.a8: There are five separate jobs in one request and no room to go deep in any. Split it into a chain: each step's output feeds the next, and you step in between them.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.quiz.q9: What goes into a system prompt?
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.quiz.a9: The two parts of the formula that don't change: role and context. Plus your standing rules. Task, constraint and format stay in the daily requests.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.recap.title: This chapter in one sentence
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.recap.p: You get what you tell me: say who I should write as, what I need to know, exactly what to do, what not to do, and in what shape to hand it over — the rest is the work you already had.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.next.title: Chapter 3 · The Agent
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.next.p: You can write the right request now. Next comes not having to write it by hand every time: flows that do the repeating work without asking you.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.guide.p: The terms used in this chapter — system prompt, context window, structured output — and the rest, on one page. In four languages.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.teach.cap: Two roads to the same result
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.teach.i5: not formal, but not sloppy either
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.teach.i6: … and a dozen things you can't put into words
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.teach.n1: You wrote ten lines and the «voice» still isn't quite right. Because you don't fully know the rules of the tone yourself — you only recognise it when you see it.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.teach.n2: You pasted a text you liked and wrote two words. Everything you couldn't describe is already inside the example — I take it from there.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.teach.fc: The left road is tiring and stays incomplete; the right one is both shorter and more accurate. The rule: if you're trying to describe a tone, stop — find something written in that tone and paste it instead.
course/chapter-2.html.ch2.fig.mock.typed: I run a small furniture workshop. Write short and direct, no jargon, and say so when you're not sure.

course/chapter-3.html.og.title: Chapter 3: The Agent — Flows that work for you 24 hours a day
